claims.text: The initial TaNbHfZrTi alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The baseline alloy is produced with minimal trace impurities through ultra-high-purity processing.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen impurities accelerate phase segregation in TaNbHfZrTi during high-temperature service.
Impurity-accelerated segregation produces brittle secondary phases.
Impurity-accelerated segregation produces depletion zones at grain boundaries.
The secondary phases and grain-boundary depletion zones reduce fracture toughness.
The secondary phases and grain-boundary depletion zones promote brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
During prolonged high-temperature exposure, oxygen and nitrogen segregate at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Oxygen and nitrogen segregation catalyzes the formation of brittle secondary phases.
The resulting depletion zones weaken solid-solution strengthening.
Weakening of solid-solution strengthening lowers fracture toughness and predisposes the alloy to brittle fracture.
After aging at approximately 700 °C, impurity-doped samples will contain more brittle secondary precipitates and depletion zones than high-purity samples.
After aging, impurity-doped samples will have lower fracture toughness than the high-purity baseline.
Impurity-doped samples will exhibit a greater prevalence of brittle intergranular fracture than the high-purity baseline.
The high-purity baseline is expected to retain a uniform single-phase solid solution during the specified exposure.
The high-purity baseline is expected to retain superior toughness under mechanical loading relative to the impurity-doped alloy.
Aging at approximately 700 °C is representative of the intended service conditions.
Impurity concentration thresholds and alternative aging regimes may alter phase-segregation dynamics and mechanical response.
